subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Nudging Healthier Eating
description: A quick, practical guide to Nudging Healthier Eating.

hook.text: Place fruit at the register and candy on the bottom shelf. Sales of fruit rise 30%. No signs, no lectures.

buildup.text: Wansink's smarter lunchroom research showed that placement, portion size, and visibility shape food choices more.

discovery.text: Smaller plates reduce calorie intake by 22%. Taller glasses make people pour less soda. Shape is a nudge.

twist.text: Labeling foods as 'healthy' backfires in some groups. They taste 'worse' when labeled healthy.

climax.text: Choice architecture in food works because eating is a System 1 behavior. We grab what's easy and visible.

punchline.text: Don't fight appetite. Redesign the plate.

quiz.question: Why do smaller plates reduce calorie intake?
options: People eat less when they feel restricted
Smaller portions look full on smaller plates, satisfying visual cues
Smaller plates change the taste of food

details.summary: Nudging healthier eating uses environmental changes like food placement, portion sizing, and menu design to steer people toward nutritious choices without restricting options.
details.whyItMatters: Diet-related diseases are a leading cause of death globally. Traditional approaches relying on education and willpower have limited success.
takeaways: Food placement at eye level increases consumption regardless of preference
Smaller plate sizes reduce portion sizes without people noticing
Healthy options listed first on menus are chosen more often

faq.question: How does food placement affect eating behavior?
faq.answer: People are three times more likely to take the first food they encounter in a serving line. Moving fruit to the front of the line and vegetables to eye level increases their consumption by 25 percent or more without any change in availability or pricing.

faq.question: Why are environmental nudges more effective than dietary education?
faq.answer: People know what they should eat but make food choices on autopilot, influenced by environmental cues. Education adds knowledge that rarely changes automatic behavior. Environmental nudges change the autopilot itself by altering what is easiest, most visible, and most convenient.
